why: Characters you never move keep their relative order and end up at the front, so they must form a prefix of reverse(s) that is also a subsequence of s. Greedy subsequence matching (two pointers) finds the longest such prefix; everything else is moved once.
hints: The characters you never touch stay in their original order. Where do they end up in the final string?

Untouched characters form the front of the result, so they must equal a prefix of reverse(s) and appear in s as a subsequence. Moved characters can be appended in any order you like to build the rest.
Two pointers: walk s and greedily match it against reverse(s). If the matched length is j, the answer is n - j. O(n) time, O(n) space for the reversed copy.
pitfalls: Greedy matching of the leftmost possible character is optimal for subsequence checks; do not try to skip matches.
Each moved character counts once, and you can choose the order you move them in.
